title: Who Is Running to Become Chicago’s Next Mayor
summary: Who Is Running to Become Chicago’s Next Mayor WTTW News Wed, 11/25/2026 - 13:20 Chicago’s next mayoral election is just months away. Sixteen candidates in October filed signatures with the Chicago Board of Election Commissioner. Mayoral candidates must submit at least 12,500 valid signatures from registered Chicago voters, and a number of candidates are facing challenges over the legitimacy of those signatures. Objections to signatures needed to be filed by Nov. 2, and the ballot is scheduled to be certified by Dec. 17, records show. Here’s a look at candidates for the Feb. 23, 2027, election. Brandon Johnson Current Job: Chicago mayor Chicago’s current mayor formally launched his campaign for reelection on Sept. 13 . Johnson said the mayoral contest would pit the “corporate class” and billionaires against the “working class” — and that he was proud to fight on the side of Chicago residents struggling to make ends meet. The former Chicago Teachers Union organizer and Cook County commissioner won in a runoff in 2023. When he announced he would run for mayor in October 2022, Johnson said he had a theory of how Chicago government could work to make it the “safest, most affordable big city in America.” “Now we know it works,” Johnson said, acknowledging he had endured “bumps and bruises.” “But our values were more threatening to the establishment than we thought.” Website: brandonforchicago.com Susana Mendoza Current Job: Illinois state comptroller Mendoza, a former state legislator and Chicago city clerk, threw her hat into the ring to become the city’s next mayor on June 3 . If elected, she said she would curb City Hall spending, rebuild trust between residents and police and ensure a safe, clean and reliable CTA transit system. Mendoza previously ran for mayor in 2019, finishing in fifth place. When Mendoza announced last year that she would not seek another term as comptroller, she said she had a “specific mission” in mind — a listening tour across Chicago to hear from residents about what they needed from the city. “I took the time to listen, time to reflect and time to decide how I could make the biggest impact on people’s lives,” Mendoza said at a campaign launch event in Little Village. Website: susanamendoza.com Mike Quigley Current Job: U.S. representative for Illinois’ 5th District The veteran Democratic legislator, who has long considered running for mayor, officially kicked off his campaign with a speech June 27 at the Uptown Theatre. Quigley has been in Congress since 2009. He has pledged to tackle Chicago’s budget issues and provide strong schools in every community, expanded mental health services and an abundant supply of housing. “It’s tough to see the city you love so much struggle in the way that we are in Chicago,” Quigley said . “The fact of the matter is, Chicago has everything it needs to succeed — its location, its people, its cultural institutions, its universities, its neighborhoods — but it’s all resting on a crumbling financial foundation.” Website: quigleyforchicago.com George Cardenas Current Job: Cook County Board of Review commissioner The longtime 12th Ward alderperson announced his plans to run for mayor June 17 , promising to fix the city’s fiscal and public safety issues. During his nearly 20 years on the Chicago City Council, Cardenas chaired its Committee on Environmental Protection and Energy and served as an ally to former Mayors Richard M. Daley, Rahm Emanuel and Lori Lightfoot. Cardenas has focused his campaign on fiscal discipline, Tax Incremental Financing reform and public safety improvements. He said his record as an elected official gives him an advantage, adding that Chicago’s current leadership has had issues with “mismanagement.” “I think Chicago is ready for someone to govern,” Cardenas said . “I think Chicago wants someone who knows the numbers, who can bring some sense into all of the spending that’s happening. … We gotta manage this whole ecosystem and make it better.” Website: cardenas4chicago.com Matt Brewer Current Job: Partner at the law firm Bartlit Beck The former Chicago Housing Authority board chair, whom Johnson sought to oust earlier this year, entered the race June 25 seeking to replace the mayor. The South Side native is not a career politician but comes with a diverse resume. He’s a co-owner of the iconic Wiener’s Circle and co-owns the city’s first Black-owned marijuana dispensary alongside his brother and mom. Brewer remains a board member on the Housing Authority. “The next mayor will step into a seat that no other mayor has stepped into where we have a fully elected school board for the first time ever, less direct control over transportation, we have a fully empowered and independent City Council that’s passed budgets around, instead of with, the mayor, and all these agencies like CHA and others who’ve become a lot more independent as well. Fractured relationships in City Council, fractured relationships in Springfield. The next mayor can’t step in and put all those genies back in the bottle,” Brewer said . “We have a new day of governance, a new day of leadership. We now need a mayor for this particular moment who can wear lots of different hats, speak different languages to different people to bring everyone together around a shared vision.” Website: mattbrewer.com Joe Holberg Current Job: Founder and CEO, Spring The Michigan-born businessman became the first candidate to officially enter the 2027 race when he kicked off his campaign last fall. The founder and CEO of Spring, a wealth advisory firm, Holberg said he will prioritize growing Chicago’s economy, eliminating debt and expanding housing options. “I’ve worked in nonprofit, I’ve worked at large companies and I even started a company and created jobs in Chicago,” Holberg said . “And I think that fresh perspective and that diversity of experiences will lend itself to being the next mayor.” Website: joeforchicago.com Lisa Nee Current Job: Healthcare and public policy advisor The former cardiologist and whistleblower launched a bid for Chicago mayor July 7. Nee began her career as a nurse and later became an interventional cardiologist. While working at Hines VA Hospital, Nee spoke out about failures in patient care that put veterans at risk. The Humboldt Park native said her priorities include making Chicago affordable for working families; trusted leadership for a safer city; and fiscal responsibility that protects the next generation from inherited debt. “I think the qualifications start with being a lifelong Chicagoan,” Nee said . “The other qualifications, though, have followed me on the journey from nurse to physician to whistleblower, breast cancer survivor, going into corporate, health equity and now really wanting to lead the city. I think it’s a combination of all of those things that you learn to navigate difficult situations but also learn where your leverage is and who your stakeholders are to get things solved for people.” Website: lisaneeforchicago.com Alexi Giannoulias Current Job: Illinois secretary of state Giannoulias entered the race for Chicago mayor on Aug. 2. He is simultaneously running for a second term as secretary of state, a position he has held since 2023. Giannoulias previously served as state treasurer for four years and unsuccessfully ran as the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in 2010. His goals for Chicago include implementing universal pre-K, raising the minimum wage and expanding affordable housing. “Chicagoans don’t expect perfection, but they do expect leadership that listens, that rolls up its sleeves to work hard, and that loves this city as much as they do,” Giannoulias said in his announcement speech , promising to lead a “government that delivers, government that demands better, and that gets things done.” Website: alexiforus.com John Kelly Current Job: Owner of All-Circo The longtime lobbyist entered the race July 28. Kelly has lobbied for the White Sox and United Center and negotiated the Bally’s agreement that opened the city’s first casino. Kelly wants the Chicago Police Department to enforce snap curfews to curb teen takeovers and said there would be 1,000 additional officers on the streets after his first year in office. Kelly wants to bring back ShotSpotter and alleges Johnson got rid of the controversial technology to hide how much crime is in the city. “Crime and safety is how someone feels,” Kelly said . “People don’t say, ‘Oh, this crime is down a certain percentage, I feel that percentage safer.’ People in the city of Chicago, they’re as safe as they feel. Speaking with them, they’re telling me they don’t feel safe. … I don’t care what crime stats people are trying to talk about. Chicago residents do not feel safe, and they tell me that every single day. That’s why I’ve made it a center point of the campaign.” Website: johnkellyforchi.com Willie Wilson Current Job: Founder, Omar Supplies, LLC On Aug. 5, Wilson announced he was making his fourth mayoral run — having previously sought the office in 2015, 2019 and 2023. The Chicago businessman and philanthropist has run for political office numerous times over the years, including a presidential campaign in 2016 and a U.S. Senate bid in 2020. Wilson, a self-made millionaire who founded a medical supply company, said he intends to focus on public safety and the economy. “You need a business person to come in and fix the city,” Wilson said . “You can’t have everything social. If you drive business out, raise taxes, jobs go away and businesses leave out. What do you have left? I’m coming in to make sure we get it right. My experience is with business, as well as community, as well as understanding people. Somebody has to do something to keep the city right and keep it going. I am Chicago.” Website: williewilson2027.com Danielle Carter-Walters Current Job: Co-founder, Chicago Flips Red Carter-Walters is a co-founder of the conservative group Chicago Flips Red. The Chicago native, who has worked as a fitness trainer, is a vocal critic of Johnson and opposes sanctuary city policies. Carter-Walters is focusing her campaign on crime, education and building what she calls a “revitalized business and industrial base.” “I’m running because I refuse to watch my hometown continue to suffer from crime, corruption, high taxes and failed leadership,” she said on her campaign website. Website: dannicformayor.com Zoe Ma Current Job: Real estate developer Ma is a real estate developer and property manager who has lived in Chicago for more than 30 years. A native of China, Ma is focusing her campaign on what she views as inequalities in the city. Ma said she wants to lower property taxes, renovate affordable homes and work to address youth poverty and homelessness. “My journey — from a working-class Muslim family in China, to student protests in Beijing, to decades of observing inequality in Chicago — has convinced me that fighting poverty requires more than words,” Ma said on her campaign website. “I am running for mayor because I believe Chicago can become a city where opportunity is shared by all.” Website: zoemaformayor.com Bill Quinlan Current Job: Attorney The longtime attorney is a Northwest Side native who previously worked on campaigns for former presidents Bill Clinton and Barack Obama; represented former CPS CEO Pedro Martinez in his effort to keep his job; and served as the state’s general counsel under then-Gov. Rod Blagojevich, resigning shortly after the governor’s arrest. Quinlan serves as chairman of the board of Lawrence Hall, which supports youth who have been victims of violence. Quinlan in September filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent fellow candidates U.S. Rep. Mike Quigley, Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias and Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas from seeking reelection while simultaneously running for mayor of Chicago. The suit argued the candidates are violating state election code, which says candidates cannot simultaneously seek two “incompatible” political offices, according to Capitol News Illinois . It was later dismissed by a judge. “What’s missing from City Hall right now is leadership,” Quinlan said in a statement. “People think of themselves. They think, how do they keep their job? How do they stay in office? We are on the brink of financial collapse that was created by politicians that were worried about getting reelected.” Website: quinlanforchicago.com Maria Pappas Current Job: Cook County treasurer After nearly 30 years as Cook County treasurer, Pappas is seeking her next gig as Chicago’s mayor. The West Virginia native, who earned her doctorate and law degree in Chicago, previously served as a Cook County commissioner. She was elected treasurer in 1998. Pappas, who is running for reelection as treasurer in the Nov. 3 general election, has said she will begin her mayoral campaign after that election. Website: mariapappas.net Failed to Qualify: Jessica “Jesse” Maronto Current Job: Traffic signal repairman, Chicago Department of Transportation Maronto failed to qualify for the ballot. She lives in the Loop and works as a traffic signal repairman for the Chicago Department of Transportation. The Oak Lawn native is a member of IBEW and vice chair of the Disability Forward CHI Employee Resource Group. Maronto campaigned on what she called a “No Poli-Tricks” platform aimed at calling out “systemic, transactional tactics.” Among her proposals are overhauling 311 to keep requests open until they are resolved; establishing a weekly payday for city workers earning less than $101,000 per year; creating safe spaces for teens with sponsored nightclubs; and addressing food deserts through public-private partnerships. Website: marontoforchicago.com John Kitover Current Job: Podcast host Kitover failed to qualify for the ballot. The U.S. Army veteran bills himself as a Libertarian focused on fiscal reform and “Chicago’s liberation.” Kitover broadcasts his views on YouTube and said he previously worked for Fortune 500 companies, the IRS and the U.S. Census Bureau. Kitover believes Chicago should address its pension debt through bankruptcy proceedings. He attempted to run for Congress in Illinois’ 16th District in the March 2026 Republican primary but was disqualified because he had just 266 valid signatures. Website: mayorkitover.com Politics

title: Army Says Explosives Detonation 'Tremendously Successful,' Early Monitoring Showing No Lead Dispersal
summary: Army Says Explosives Detonation 'Tremendously Successful,' Early Monitoring Showing No Lead Dispersal Patty Wetli Wed, 11/25/2026 - 09:15 The U.S. Army has conducted a controlled detonation of nearly 10,000 pounds of explosive lead azide Wednesday at approximately 9 a.m. at a munitions plant in Middletown, Iowa. In an update late Wednesday morning, Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, who is leading the operation in Iowa, called the detonation “tremendously successful” and said it had “wildly exceeded expectations.” There were no secondary explosions and all of the lead azide was destroyed, reducing to as close to zero as possible the threat of an uncontrolled blast, Shirley said. Residents closest to the blast site were told to evacuate, and there is a potential for lead dust to spread southwest into neighboring Missouri. A shift in wind direction from the original detonation date of Nov. 20 has taken Illinois out of the path of dispersal. Early monitoring has thus far detected zero levels of lead in the air, officials said. The detonation did not produce an earth shaking event or release a large cloud of debris, with observers on the scene heard asking, “That was it?” during a livestream. Local reporters with KCCI-TV in Des Moines said the blast was “not as visible as maybe we expected.” A New York Times reporter positioned a half-mile from the site described the sound as “dull booms,” like thunder. An initial cloud of smoke dissipated quickly. Lee Zeldin, administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, told CNN in a live interview the Army was “very happy” with the results. Earlier this year, inspectors identified degradation of the lead azide, making it ultra-sensitive to minimal friction, vibration, heat or shock, creating a risk of an unexpected explosion. After an “exhaustive evaluation” of alternatives, the decision was made to carry out a controlled detonation, Shirley said at a news conference Tuesday. That decision was communicated to residents of Middletown, but the information was not widely shared elsewhere. Many Iowans, Illinois and Missourians were caught completely off guard about the potential for lead exposure when the U.S. EPA issued a permit for the blast's initial detonation date. Public outcry and legal filings pushed the detonation back, but Army officials have maintained throughout that the blast is the safest way to neutralize the lead azide. “I’ve seen the reporting on the chemical neutralization agent. That proved to be an unsafe method,” Col. Aaron Teller, group commander, 71st Explosive Ordnance Disposal, told the media. "We’ve observed a significant accumulation of crystallized lead azide on the exterior of the barrels, including the barrel lids. It prevents those barrels from being able to be moved. It prevents us from removing the barrel lids. That’s why they can’t be treated, and that’s why you can’t open the lids to treat it with a chemical neutralization agent.” In advance of the detonation, the EPA has sent hundreds of staff to the area and has collected more than 1,200 total samples of soil, dust, air and water to test for lead levels and will monitor conditions during and after the explosion. EPA’s air monitoring will be reporting data points every five minutes, the agency said. In response to a query from WTTW News, the EPA said it is fielding numerous requests regarding whether this sampling protocol had been in place prior to the original detonation date. The agency did not provide an answer. The U.S. Army has ramped up its mitigation efforts in recent days as well. — The barrels are stored in concrete bunkers barricaded with sand-filled barriers two stories high; — Aqueous foam blocks, two walls of four 16,000-gallon water tanks, and gel blocks adjacent to the bunkers are expected to absorb thermal energy and reduce airborne particulate emissions directly at the blast source. — PFAS-free suppressing foam is being applied over containment screens and tarps to submerge the structures. High-volume industrial misting units and water sprayers will thoroughly saturate the soil and airspace before and during detonation, ensuring escaping particles are immediately weighed down by water and deposited back onto the soil inside the secure installation footprint. Adam Telle, acting secretary of the U.S. Army, told the Associated Press that the Army is reviewing its weapons storage facilities to ensure something like this never happens again. This is a developing story. Check back for updates. Contact Patty Wetli: pwetli@wttw.com Politics

title: City Council to Weigh Paying $4.6M to Man Who Spent 13 Years in Prison After Wrongful Murder Conviction
summary: City Council to Weigh Paying $4.6M to Man Who Spent 13 Years in Prison After Wrongful Murder Conviction Heather Cherone Wed, 11/25/2026 - 12:56 Chicago taxpayers should pay $4.6 million to a man who spent 13 years in prison after he was wrongfully convicted of murdering a man during a robbery in 1990, city lawyers recommended. Willie Sorrell, 65, was shot and killed on Dec. 21, 1990, when two men attempted to rob the driver of a bread truck in South Austin. The driver fired at the would-be robbers, who returned fire. Sorrell, a bystander, was fatally wounded, records show. Sorrell’s killing went unsolved until 2002, when Chicago Police Detectives Jerome Bogucki and Raymond Schalk reinterviewed witnesses to Sorrell’s murder after they had been arrested on separate charges. Both identified James Fletcher as the gunman who killed Sorrell. At the time, Fletcher was imprisoned after being convicted of armed robbery. No physical evidence linked Fletcher to Sorrell’s murder. Fletcher was convicted of Sorrell’s murder in 2005 and sentenced to life in prison without parole. The Chicago City Council’s Finance Committee will consider resolving the lawsuit Fletcher filed in 2023 on Monday. A final vote of the City Council could come as soon as Dec. 8. One of the witnesses recanted her identification of Fletcher in 2011, telling investigators that detectives told her to identify Fletcher as the gunman. After she did so, the charges pending against her were dropped, she said. Fletcher’s conviction was overturned in 2019. The Cook County State’s Attorney’s Office declined to retry him in 2020 and he was released. Fletcher was granted a certificate of innocence in 2022, records show. Bogucki and Schalk have been accused of misconduct in several other lawsuits alleging they improperly forced witnesses to crimes to identify innocent suspects, including Thaddeus Jimenez, who was 13 years old when he was convicted of murder based on evidence gathered by both detectives. A jury awarded Jimenez $25 million in damages in 2012 after he sued the city for wrongful conviction. In 2017, Jimenez was sentenced to nine years in prison after using that money to rebuild the Simon City Royals street gang. In 2025, the City Council agreed to pay $18.5 million to Francisco “Frankie” Benitez, who spent 34 years in prison after being convicted of a 1989 double murder he didn’t commit. Fletcher’s lawsuit also names former Chicago Police Detective Anthony Wojcik, who retired in 2016 while under investigation by the Chicago Office of the Inspector General for his role in the investigation of the 2014 shooting death of Laquan McDonald by Chicago Police Officer Jason Van Dyke. Since the start of 2026, it has cost Chicago taxpayers more than $219 million to resolve dozens of lawsuits brought by people wrongfully convicted based on evidence gathered by the Chicago Police Department, according to an analysis of city data by WTTW News. Taxpayers will pay an additional $260.8 million in 2027 and 2028 to 17 men who sued the city after being wrongfully convicted based on evidence developed by former Chicago Police Detective Reynaldo Guevara. Fletcher is represented by attorney Jennifer Blagg and the law firm of Loevy and Loevy, which also represented the men who resolved their cases against the city and Guevara. The firm advertises itself by telling potential clients that “no law firm in Chicago has been more successful in litigating police brutality and police misconduct cases.” The City Council’s Finance Committee is also scheduled to weigh whether to pay $400,000 to resolve a separate lawsuit filed by a man who was convicted of killing a man in 2013 and was later acquitted of all charges during a new trial. Jonathon Hoskins was shot and killed in Park Manor while talking with a group of friends in April 2013, records show. Phillip Anderson was convicted of his murder in 2016, only to have his conviction vacated on appeal after a witness testified officers pressured him to identify Anderson as the shooter. A new jury declared him not guilty in 2024, records show. Note: Loevy and Loevy has done legal work for WTTW News around Freedom of Information Act requests. WTTW News coverage of policing and police reform is supported by The Joyce Foundation. Contact Heather Cherone: @HeatherCherone | (773) 569-1863 | hcherone@wttw.com Crime & Law Politics

title: Do You Feel Safe on the CTA? New NORC/WTTW News Survey Shows How Chicago’s Racial, Geographic Divides Affect Experience
summary: Do You Feel Safe on the CTA? New NORC/WTTW News Survey Shows How Chicago’s Racial, Geographic Divides Affect Experience Nick Blumberg Wed, 11/25/2026 - 05:00 Chicago’s long-standing racial, ethnic and geographic divides have a dramatic impact on how safe passengers feel while riding the CTA, a recent public opinion poll shows. The survey, conducted by the nonpartisan research organization NORC at the University of Chicago and commissioned by WTTW News, asked more than 1,100 adults how safe they feel on CTA buses and trains. It comes as transit officials and law enforcement have touted major improvements in public safety and mapped out big changes in the years ahead — and after years of high-profile incidents, wavering public perception, and attacks from the Trump administration alleging failures to protect passengers and employees. White respondents reported the highest levels of feeling safe (65% on buses and 51% on trains) compared to Black respondents (23% on buses and 16% on trains) and respondents identified by the survey as Hispanic (28% on buses and 27% on trains). Geography also highlights the differing feelings of safety among transit riders. Respondents from the North Central region reported feeling safest (64% on buses and 48% on trains) while those from the South (24% on buses and 15% on trains) and Southwest (32% and 26% on trains) were the lowest. The poll was conducted Sept. 13-23, using a sample drawn from NORC’s probability-based ChicagoSpeaks Panel, which is designed to be representative of the Chicago population. The margin of sampling error is plus or minus 4.1 percentage points. “Every rider and employee deserves to feel safe on public transit, regardless of their ZIP code, ethnicity, or travel needs,” Northern Illinois Transit Authority Interim Executive Director Jamie Rhee told WTTW News in a statement. “NITA is taking critical steps to restore rider confidence and make meaningful investments in public safety. … Improving safety will take sustained effort, but these initiatives represent concrete steps toward making transit safer and more welcoming for everyone.” For its part, a CTA spokesperson told WTTW News that in 2026 the agency “has implemented an expanded safety approach that’s designed to help every rider feel welcome on public transit. This includes the increased presence of both law enforcement and non-law enforcement social services outreach teams, and physical and environmental upgrades at stations.” Among those efforts is a new security plan rolled out in the spring amid attacks from the Trump-appointed leader of the Federal Transit Administration, which threatened to withhold funding from CTA and alleged that the agency failed its responsibility to “creat(e) a safe, reliable transit system.” And thanks to additional state funding secured as part of the law that created NITA, CTA said it’s been able to increase policing hours on buses and trains by 75% in partnership with the Chicago Police Department and Cook County Sheriff’s Office Police. The Sheriff’s office said so far it’s netted 276 arrests, including 160 felony arrests and nearly 11,000 blocked attempts to evade paying a fare. Cook County Sheriff Tom Dart told WTTW News that fare jumping is a likely indicator of other antisocial behavior. “If that’s your initial step in your journey, what do you think the chances are that person’s overly concerned about smoking on the train, drinking on the train, using loud music on the train?” Dart said earlier this year in an interview about the new transit missions . “It all sort of feeds into it.” For its part, the Cook County State’s Attorney’s Office has also made transit crime a priority, seeking pretrial detention for those accused of violent acts on public transportation and standing up a new task force with specialized training. “The task force is comprised of state’s attorneys from across the office, all who have specialties in different disciplines,” Yvette Loizon, chief assistant state’s attorney of policy and external affairs, said in an April appearance on “ Chicago Tonight .” “The idea is that we will have those state’s attorneys specially trained so that they know all of the information that they need to to effectively and efficiently prosecute CTA crime.” Increased police presence on transit has been the subject of much public outcry, in particular after several high-profile incidents on the system. In November of last year, Bethany MaGee was doused in gasoline and set on fire on a Blue Line train in an apparently random attack . Last month, CTA janitor Julian Mobley was fatally stabbed at the Damen Green Line station. Tom Kotarac, chair of the NITA Board of Directors, told WTTW News that Mobley’s killing is “an absolute wake-up call to all of us across the system to make this the top priority. We are not doing enough and we need to do more, and the General Assembly acknowledged that and the governor acknowledged that when they created the Northern Illinois Transit Authority.” “Our investment in police has been under what was necessary,” said Roberto Requejo, a senior fellow at the Center for Community Investment and a former member of the CTA Board of Directors. “When you compare with other cities around the world, it was a very limited presence of police in the system — and also very little, almost no partnerships with community-based organizations, social service organizations, and other approaches that are not law enforcement.” To that end, NITA’s proposed 2027 budget includes more than $54 million in safety improvements that include a Ride Safe incident reporting app; creating an Office of Transit Safety and Experience; launching the transit ambassador program; and better coordination between law enforcement and social service providers. Requejo said CTA has come a long way in developing partnerships with outside groups, including social service organizations launching direct outreach missions to people sheltering on trains. And the agency just launched a Safe Ride Specialist pilot program aimed at de-escalating potentially dangerous situations and aiding riders with mental health or substance use issues. But Requejo stressed that law enforcement and non-law enforcement interventions alike must take into account Chicago’s racial and geographic segregation. “For any approach to safety, you have to lead with an equity lens, and what that means is that you cannot have a one-size-fits-all approach. It has to depend on the type of community, the type of riders that you are working to keep safe,” he said. Overall, respondents to the survey reported feeling safer on buses (42%) than on trains (33%). Respondents aged 60 and older reported the lowest levels of feeling safe (35% on buses and 21% on trains). A majority of male and female respondents reported feeling safe on buses but unsafe on trains; a higher percentage of male respondents than female reported feeling safe on both forms of transit. The results may also demonstrate that taking transit more regularly can affect feelings of safety. NITA shared results of its own quarterly panel survey, which factors in whether someone is a regular rider, and said its second quarter results showed an average 9.5% increase on public safety metrics from the end of last year. (The NORC and WTTW News survey did not ask respondents about how often they take buses and trains.) Audrey Wennink, a senior director at the Metropolitan Planning Council, said the increase in law enforcement transit missions has been driving results, with officers focusing on areas of particular concern as a guiding principle. “I think there’s going to be a real focus on making data-driven decisions, creating the systems where problems that are reported are followed up on and progressive changes are measured,” Wennink said. She also touted the transit ambassador program rolling out next year, which is mandated by the law that created NITA. “We need various different types of professionals to deal with very different situations,” Wennink said. “We want people to be safe and we want crime not to happen on transit, but we also don’t want to over-police transit and have people feel like they’re in a kind of police state either. So it’s a delicate balance.” Kyle Lucas, executive director of Better Streets Chicago, said CTA has made important strides in recent years to address public safety and rider experience. And while transit can play a role in addressing violent crime, homelessness, or substance use problems, Lucas cautioned that it needs to be a shared responsibility. “It really cannot be all up to the transit agencies to solve all of society’s problems,” Lucas said. “All of these are situations that are happening across the city of Chicago, whether it’s in transit or not. It’s just a convergence of societal issues … our housing crisis, or (the) mental health crisis in the city, and so I think it’s really important that our city, county and state leaders step up.” Transit advocates also said that improving the physical environment can make riders and employees safer — and that doesn’t just mean clean, bright and welcoming stations and stops. Requejo told WTTW News it’s important to think about the communities that surround stations, many of which have vacant land. “You cannot quantify that, but you clearly feel safer in a place where there’s good lighting, and there is greenery, and there is a restaurant nearby or there’s a coffee shop, versus waiting at a station or a bus stop where there’s a vacant lot or derelict property,” said Requejo, former executive director of Elevated Chicago, which advocates for equitable transit-oriented development. 2027’s NITA budget has money set aside to encourage development around transit, which Requejo is encouraged by — but he cautioned that money alone doesn’t constitute a development strategy. “I do encourage NITA to take this as seriously as they are taking safety or frequency or cleanliness, and establish an agenda for development that is a model for the region and for the country, and not an afterthought,” Requejo said. While CTA has touted significant improvements in ridership and reductions in crime, the public perception of safety on transit can be a difficult needle to move. Lucas said clear, consistent messaging is key, both from transit leaders and advocates. And he added that as passengers start to see things like safe ride specialists and transit ambassadors, they’ll likely feel a shift in their daily commute. “People’s perspective didn’t change overnight about whether or not transit was safe,” Lucas said. “It’s something that will take time.” WTTW News coverage of policing and police reform is supported by The Joyce Foundation. title: Illinois Will Not Participate in Federal Scholarship Tax Credit Program, Pritzker Announces
summary: Illinois Will Not Participate in Federal Scholarship Tax Credit Program, Pritzker Announces Eunice Alpasan Wed, 11/25/2026 - 09:48 In a closely watched decision, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker decided that the state will not opt into a federal scholarship tax credit program that is set to begin next year, according to a Tuesday announcement. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, the federal scholarship tax credit program would allow individuals to donate up to $1,700 to an authorized scholarship-granting organization in a participating state in order to receive a federal tax credit of the same amount in exchange. The federal scholarship tax credit was signed into law last year as part of HR1, or President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” Trump administration officials said the tax credit establishes the nation’s first nationwide school choice program , with the program expected to further fuel the school choice movement. “At a time when public school education needs investments more than ever, we should not siphon money from public schools for private education — especially as the Trump Administration’s policies decimate education,” Pritzker said in the written announcement. At least 30 states have opted into the program, including Democratic governors Kathy Hochul of New York and Jared Polis of Colorado. Illinois joins states such as Arizona, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Oregon and Virginia whose governors have decided to not participate in the program. Scholarship-granting organizations in each participating state would decide how much to grant to students who apply, depending on available funds and need. Scholarships can be used to cover education expenses for private, public and charter schools, including tutoring and special education services. Elementary through high school students qualify if their families earn up to three times the area’s median income. In its announcement, Pritzker’s office said federal regulations prohibit states from setting strict guidelines and standards on the organizations handing out scholarships. Pritzker argued the program would use taxpayer funding to subsidize donations to private schools that could discriminate based on religion, sexual orientation or other characteristics — while diverting attention and resources away from Illinois students attending public schools. About 1.8 million students in Illinois attend public schools, according to the governor’s office. In addition, the governor's office said the tax credit diverts funds from federal revenue, and argued that the program's wide income eligibility range means that the primary benefactors of the program will not be children from under-resourced households. Pritzker’s decision was being closely watched by education advocates, who have debated the program’s potential impacts and whether the state should opt-in. Even though the state has not opted in, Illinois taxpayers can still donate to scholarship-granting organizations in a participating state in order to receive the federal tax credit. The Illinois Federation of Teachers and the Chicago Teachers Union applauded Pritzker’s decision. “Public dollars belong in public schools,“ IFT and CTU President Stacy Davis Gates said in a Tuesday statement. ”Trump’s voucher scheme was built to pull money out of public education with zero oversight and zero educational benefit for students. Illinois' 1.8 million public school students deserve better, and today they got it." The Associated Press contributed to this report. Contact Eunice Alpasan: ealpasan@wttw.com Education

title: Marching Illini Set To Deliver Epic Ode to Chicago During Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Parade: Watch Rehearsal
summary: Marching Illini Set To Deliver Epic Ode to Chicago During Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Parade: Watch Rehearsal Patty Wetli Wed, 11/25/2026 - 15:27 The University of Illinois’ Marching Illini earned a coveted performing spot during this year’s 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade and if rehearsals are any indication, their song selection will be a love letter to the band’s home state. Video posted on social media of Tuesday’s run-through in New York City captured the band’s 400 members practicing an epic rendition of Sufjan Stevens’ “Chicago,” a soaring ode to the city from the singer-songwriter’s 2005 album “Illinois.” “This band’s rehearsal gave me goosebumps,” a bystander shared on Instagram. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Lex (@lexiconoflove) The parade had been set to kick off at 7:30 a.m. Central time on Thanksgiving Day, but is being postponed for the first time in decades due to an impending nor’easter bearing down on the East Coast. The parade is now scheduled for Saturday. The 10 marching bands chosen for the centennial anniversary parade will perform along the 2½-mile parade route lined with an anticipated 3 million spectators. The payoff comes in the form of a 1 minute and 15 second television slot, band director Barry Houser said in a 2025 interview , when the Marching Illini’s selection was announced . It will be the band’s second-ever appearance in the Macy’s parade. The first came in 2015, when the band was given prime position marching in front of Santa Claus. title: Pay $10M to Man Who Spent 20 Years in Prison After Being Wrongfully Convicted, City Lawyers Recommend
summary: Pay $10M to Man Who Spent 20 Years in Prison After Being Wrongfully Convicted, City Lawyers Recommend Heather Cherone Wed, 11/25/2026 - 11:20 Chicago taxpayers should pay $10 million to a man who spent 20 years in prison after he was wrongfully convicted of murdering a man in July 2000, city lawyers recommended. Jeremy Jackson was 16 when 32-year-old Mitchell Dotson was fatally shot while standing on a street corner on the West Side, a slaying that was unsolved until January 2001 when another teen said he and Jackson were responsible for the murder. The City Council’s Finance Committee will consider resolving the lawsuit Jackson filed in 2023 on Monday. A final vote of the City Council could come as soon as Dec. 8. After being interrogated by Chicago police detectives for eight hours without a parent present, as required by Illinois law, Jackson signed a statement confessing to the crime. Jackson later said he confessed after being slapped by a detective and forced to sign blank pieces of paper to which detectives later added a confession. The lead detective investigating Dotson’s murder was Anthony Wojcik, who retired in 2016 while under investigation by the Chicago Office of the Inspector General for his role in the investigation of the 2014 shooting death of Laquan McDonald by Chicago Police Officer Jason Van Dyke. Former Inspector General Joseph Ferguson said he would have recommended Wojcik’s termination after determining he improperly disposed of police reports documenting the statements of witnesses to the teen’s shooting and found that Wojcik “authored and approved” false statements that “served to exaggerate the threat that McDonald posed,” records show. Jackson’s lawyer, who was disbarred in 2008 after officials found he committed “serious misconduct” in nine other criminal cases, never asked the judge in Jackson’s case to exclude his confession from evidence because it was illegally obtained, records show. No physical evidence linked Jackson to Dotson’s murder, although Jackson testified he was walking to his sister’s home when the shooting took place, records show. Jackson was convicted of Dotson’s murder in 2002 and sentenced to 50 years in prison, records show. He was later re-sentenced to 35 years in prison because of his age at the time of the murder, records show. Jackson’s conviction was overturned in 2022 and he was released. The Cook County State’s Attorney’s Office declined to retry him, and he was granted a certificate of innocence in 2023, records show. Since the start of 2026, it has cost Chicago taxpayers more than $219 million to resolve dozens of lawsuits brought by people wrongfully convicted based on evidence gathered by the Chicago Police Department, according to an analysis of city data by WTTW News. Taxpayers will pay an additional $260.8 million in 2027 and 2028 to 17 men who sued the city after being wrongfully convicted based on evidence developed by former Chicago Police Detective Reynaldo Guevara. Jackson is represented by the law firm of Loevy and Loevy, which also represented the men who resolved their cases against the city and Guevara, and attorney Jennifer Blagg. The firm advertises itself by telling potential clients that “no law firm in Chicago has been more successful in litigating police brutality and police misconduct cases.” Note: Loevy and Loevy has done legal work for WTTW News around Freedom of Information Act requests.
